```{r include=FALSE,echo=FALSE}
require(tigerstats)
require(tidyverse)
mydata <- read.csv(file="pushups.csv")
```

# Introduction

This report asks whether Georgetown College football players at line positions and skill positions have the same average number of push-ups. The data are the `pushups` dataset from the `tigerstats` package, supplied in this project as `pushups.csv`. Two players asked their teammates to do as many push-ups as they could in two minutes. There are 30 players. Each row records body weight in pounds, the number of push-ups completed, and position. Position has two categories: `LINE` (positions that require high body mass) and `SKILL` (positions that require a lot of running).

The question is a comparison of a numerical response, push-ups, across a categorical grouping variable, position. The hypotheses are:

$H_0$: There is no difference between the average number of pushups of line vs skill players.

$H_A$: The average number of pushups done by line players is statistically different than that of skill players.

# Methods

Position is categorical, with levels LINE and SKILL. The number of push-ups is numerical. This is a categorical-versus-numerical question with two groups, so the comparison of averages uses a two-sample *t*-test.

The descriptive part of the report has two pieces. A side-by-side boxplot shows the center and spread of push-ups in each position. A numerical summary gives the sample size, five-number summary, mean, and standard deviation for each group.

The inferential test is Welch's two-sample *t*-test of `pushups` by `position`. The alternative hypothesis is two-sided, because it says the averages are different and does not state which group is higher. Welch's test compares means and does not require the two groups to have the same variance. That choice fits these data: the groups are unequal in size, and the numerical summary shows that skill players are more spread out than line players. The significance level is 0.05.

The test treats the 30 players as independent observations. It also relies on the push-up counts within each position being roughly normal, or at least not so skewed that the mean is a poor summary. Those conditions are checked against the boxplot and the group sizes in the results.

# Results

<!--Divide this section into two sub-sections: One for your descriptive results and one for your inferential results.!-->

## Descriptive Results

### Graphical Descriptive Results

The boxplot below compares the numerical push-up counts for the two position categories. Under the null hypothesis the two boxes would have similar centers. They do not. The skill box sits well above the line box, and the two boxes do not overlap. A typical skill player completed more push-ups in two minutes than a typical line player. Line players are packed into a low, narrow range. Skill players are higher and more spread out, including one very high value.

```{r}
boxplot(
  pushups ~ position,
  data = mydata,
  main = "Push-ups by football position",
  xlab = "Position",
  ylab = "Push-ups in two minutes",
  col = c("#9ecae1", "#a1d99b")
)
```

This graph is aimed at the hypothesis under test. It shows a large separation in the center of the push-up distribution, with skill players higher. That pattern is what a difference in averages would look like. The graph does not by itself give the probability of a difference this large if the null hypothesis were true. That probability comes from the *t*-test in the inferential section.

### Numerical Descriptive Results

The table reports the sample size and the usual numerical summaries of push-ups for each position. These numbers describe the same comparison the boxplot shows, in a form that can be tied directly to the averages named in the hypotheses.

```{r}
group_stats <- function(x) {
  c(
    n = length(x),
    min = min(x),
    Q1 = as.numeric(quantile(x, 0.25)),
    median = median(x),
    Q3 = as.numeric(quantile(x, 0.75)),
    max = max(x),
    mean = mean(x),
    sd = sd(x)
  )
}
stats_table <- aggregate(pushups ~ position, data = mydata, group_stats)
stats_table <- cbind(
  position = stats_table$position,
  as.data.frame(stats_table$pushups)
)
stats_table
```

Eight players are line players and 22 are skill players. The mean number of push-ups is 17.1 for line players and 49.7 for skill players, so the sample averages differ by about 32.6 push-ups. The medians tell the same story: 14.5 for line players and 47.5 for skill players. The middle half of the line group runs from 10.3 to 24.3 push-ups, while the middle half of the skill group runs from 31.3 to 57.5. Skill players are also more variable (standard deviation 23.0 versus 9.7), and the highest skill count is 108.

Relative to the hypothesis, the numerical results show that the skill average is much higher than the line average in this sample. The unequal standard deviations are why the inferential test does not assume equal variances. These summaries describe the observed players. They do not yet give the probability of a gap this large if the two position groups actually had the same average.

## Inferential Results

The hypotheses tested here are the ones stated in the introduction.

$H_0$: the mean number of push-ups is the same for line players and skill players.

$H_A$: the mean number of push-ups differs between line players and skill players.

Welch's two-sample *t*-test is appropriate because push-ups are numerical, position is categorical with two levels, and the standard deviations are not the same. The code below estimates the difference in means (line minus skill), the *t* statistic, the degrees of freedom, the two-sided *p*-value, and a 95% confidence interval.

```{r}
t.test(pushups ~ position, data = mydata)
```

The test statistic is $t = -5.43$ on $27.08$ degrees of freedom. The negative sign means the line mean is below the skill mean. The sample means are 17.13 push-ups for line players and 49.73 push-ups for skill players. The 95% confidence interval for the line mean minus the skill mean is $(-44.91, -20.29)$. The interval does not contain 0, so the data support a lower line average. Skill players average about 20 to 45 more push-ups than line players.

The *p*-value is $9.421 \times 10^{-6}$, or 0.000009421. If the null hypothesis were true, and line and skill players had the same average number of push-ups, the probability of observing a difference in sample means at least this large is 0.000009421. That is about 9 chances in a million. A difference this extreme would almost never show up by chance alone when there is truly no difference in averages. Because that probability is far below 0.05, we reject $H_0$. The average number of push-ups for line players is statistically different from the average for skill players, and the estimates show that the skill average is higher.

This procedure fits the question for these reasons:

- The response is numerical and the grouping variable is categorical with exactly two groups, which is the setting for a two-sample *t*-test of means.
- The players are separate people, so the observations are treated as independent.
- Welch's version does not assume equal variances. The group standard deviations, 9.7 and 23.0, and the unequal sample sizes, 8 and 22, make that the right version.
- The line sample is small ($n = 8$), and one skill player completed 108 push-ups. The boxplot still shows the whole skill group shifted upward, and the skill median (47.5) remains far above the line median (14.5), so the mean difference is not an artifact of a single point. The counts within each group are close enough to symmetric for a comparison of means.


# Discussion and Conclusion

We reject the null hypothesis. Line players and skill players do not have the same average number of push-ups. If the averages were truly the same, the probability of a sample difference at least this large is 0.000009421. Skill players did more push-ups: about 49.7 on average, compared with about 17.1 for line players.

That difference should not be read as proof that playing a skill position causes a player to do more push-ups. Position was not assigned by the study. Line positions are the ones that require high body mass, and skill positions are the ones that require more running, so the two groups already differ in the kind of athlete who plays them. Body weight, training, or both could sit behind the push-up gap. The result does answer the question that was asked: in this team, the average number of push-ups for skill players is statistically different from, and higher than, the average for line players.
